title: Two Giant Black Holes From Long Ago
summary: Scientists have found two huge black holes shining side by side. They come from a time just 900 million years after the Big Bang. Each one is so big that scientists do not know how it grew so fast. The pair has a Hawaiian name, Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua. The two black holes sit about 18,100 light-years apart, about one-fifth as wide as our Milky Way galaxy. One weighs about 1.5 billion times as much as the Sun. The other weighs about 400 million Suns. A black hole gives off no light by itself. But when gas and stars fall toward it, the stuff heats up and glows very brightly. It can outshine every star in its galaxy. Scientists call that glowing area a quasar. Finding quasar pairs is hard. A black hole shines as a quasar for only a short time, and very old quasars are faint and close together in the sky. This is only the third pair ever found from the early time called cosmic dawn. The James Webb Space Telescope and the Gemini North telescope in Hawai'i found it. The work was led by Silvia Onorato and published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
why_it_matters: Looking at these black holes is like looking back in time to when the Universe was young.

background_read: A black hole is a place in space where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.
When gas and stars fall toward a black hole, the stuff heats up and glows, and scientists call that bright area a quasar.
Big telescopes let scientists see light from very far away and long ago.
